lead.kicker: TOP STORY  •  YEMEN AND SAUDI ARABIA
lead.headline: Riyadh's Airport Stays Shut as Yemen's War Spills Over
lead.deck: Saudi Arabia reports a new barrage of drones and missiles, and Washington weighs joining in.
body: Think of Yemen's war as a fight inside one house that has now spread next door. Yemen's internationally recognised government is fighting the Houthis, a movement backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia, Yemen's neighbour, backs the government with an air campaign. The Houthis have now hit back at Saudi Arabia itself. Saudi Arabia has reportedly carried out hundreds of strikes on Houthi-held areas, including the capital Sanaa, and the Houthis have declared Saudi airspace a zone of military operations.

On Saturday 10 October they struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said at least 12 people were killed and at least 309 wounded. The dead came from many countries, including Bangladesh, the US, Jordan, Syria, Sudan and Egypt. It was the third Houthi attack on that airport in one week. The Saudi-led coalition called it a war crime.

On 12 October Saudi Arabia reported a new barrage of drones and missiles, and Riyadh's airport remains shut. President Trump says he is considering joining the Saudi-led offensive, which aims to push the Houthis from Yemen's Red Sea coast. A Houthi leader warned of a swift and painful response if the US does. Iran says it is ready to help facilitate talks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

The human cost is rising on both sides of the border. The UN says more than 217,000 people have been displaced since fighting escalated on Yemen's west coast, and a UN envoy has warned that Yemen has returned to full-scale war. Yemen's Saudi-backed government says Houthi strikes over 24 hours killed at least five civilians and wounded over a dozen, including in an attack on a hospital in Taiz.

world.headline: An 'Energy Ceasefire' That Both Sides Deny
world.deck: Ukraine says it has held back from hitting Russian energy sites; Russia's strikes go on.
body: Imagine two players agreeing to stop hitting each other's power supply while the rest of the game goes on. That is the idea of an energy ceasefire. On Sunday 11 October President Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to one, effective immediately. By Monday both sides had denied it.

Ukraine's President Zelenskyy told a forum in Warsaw that Ukraine had refrained from attacking Russian energy sites since the announcement, and that Russia kept attacking Ukraine's. A Russian strike on a residential high-rise in a Kyiv suburb killed at least two people on Monday evening.

US envoys told Ukrainian officials that a deal letting Russia export diesel is meant to draw Moscow back to talks, though they said Mr Putin was not ready to negotiate an end to the war. In the Strait of Hormuz, an oil tanker was hit by a projectile on Monday, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed the attack. It said it was the third ship it had hit in two days, and at least 18 attacks on ships in or near the strait have occurred since the start of October.
Sixty countries, including EU members, Australia and the UK, backed a declaration pledging to preserve freedom of navigation and opposing tolls on straits used for international navigation.

On the battlefield, Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi, the former commander-in-chief of Ukraine's forces, told the BBC that Ukraine has stabilised the front line and broken Russia's ability to advance. Russia's Defence Ministry said it hit targets in Ukraine including vessels carrying military cargo, and did not mention energy sites.

uk.headline: Burnham Blames Iran's Revolutionary Guard for the RAF Fairford Plot
uk.deck: Iran's ambassador rejects the claim and has been summoned.
body: RAF Fairford is a Royal Air Force base in Gloucestershire. Five British nationals, all in their mid-20s, were arrested near the base on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism, and later bailed under investigation. Police said petrol, but no explosive devices, was found in the vans.

On Monday Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Parliament that Iran's Revolutionary Guard was almost certainly behind a suspected plot to attack the base. It was the first official UK blame for the alleged attack. Earlier he had spoken of strong indications of Iranian involvement.
Iran's ambassador, Seyed Ali Mousavi, categorically rejects the accusation. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband summoned him. No charges have been announced.
uk.why: A government naming another state in a plot is a serious step, so it matters that the police investigation is still going and the accused country denies it.
also: France: the navy boarded the tanker DF Peak south of Reunion, which it suspects of carrying fuel for Russia's shadow fleet.
Economy: Chancellor John Healey plans his first Budget on 28 October.

europe.headline: Drones Hit Two Ships Off Bulgaria
europe.deck: Eleven sailors are missing after one ship sank.
body: Bulgaria sits on the western shore of the Black Sea. Its Prime Minister, Rumen Radev, says drones struck two ships off the coast, and one sank. Rescuers evacuated 15 crew, one sailor was rescued from the sunken ship, and 11 sailors are missing.

The 15 evacuated were seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis. Bulgaria summoned Russia's ambassador without formally accusing Russia. Mr Radev said there is no solid evidence against a specific party, but that the outcome favours Russia. He called the attacks completely unacceptable.

Bulgaria is not alone in worrying. Czech intelligence chief Michal Koudelka said Russia could pursue riskier operations in NATO states that support Ukraine within months. NATO's top commander, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, said the alliance would be ready to fight tonight if attacked.

europe.why: The Black Sea is shared by countries on both sides of the war, so attacks on ships near NATO and EU member Bulgaria raise tension in Europe.
europe.analyst: Why might Bulgaria avoid naming who is responsible? What would count as solid evidence? How could shipping be protected without widening the war?
